messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 33
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Social Media Manager
- Trauma Type: Relief worker in war zone
- Pcl5: 68

He first went to the war zone at 31, after years of working in communications and feeling, by his own account, that he was good at staying calm when other people were not. As a social media manager, he had spent much of his adult life shaping stories, choosing images, and helping organizations speak clearly under pressure. When a relief agency offered him short-term work managing outreach for a humanitarian response, he said yes quickly. He remembers feeling proud to be useful in a place where so many people were frightened and exhausted. His wife was nervous about the assignment, but he reassured her that he would be in a secure compound and that his role was mainly behind a screen.

That belief does not hold for long. Within days, he is hearing gunfire at night and seeing injured families arrive at the field site covered in dust and blood. The first memory he returns to again and again is of a child brought in after an attack on a village. He remembers the child’s small shoes, one still tied, and the silence in the room when the team realizes there is nothing more they can do. He is not the one providing medical care, but he feels as if he is witnessing everything. He says that in the beginning he keeps telling himself to focus on the work: post the updates, translate the messages, reassure donors, keep the phones charged, keep the story moving. But the images he is trying to organize for others begin to arrange themselves inside him.

As the weeks pass, the danger becomes ordinary in the way that terrifies him most. He learns the sound of incoming shelling, the difference between nearby and far away, the exact moment the camp goes quiet before panic starts. He watches colleagues flinch at every loud noise. He starts sleeping in short stretches, shoes on, phone in hand. He avoids looking directly at the bodies of those who die before help arrives, but he cannot avoid the smell of the clinic tent or the sound of grieving families outside. He finds himself feeling numb during the day and flooded at night. When he calls his wife, he keeps his voice light and tells her he is managing well. He does not tell her that sometimes he sits on the edge of his cot unable to remember what year it is, or that he has started pressing his palms into his thighs to prove to himself that he is still present.

There is one night that remains fixed in him. A convoy is delayed, and a checkpoint becomes violent. He is not in the vehicle that is hit, but he is close enough to hear the shooting and see the aftermath when survivors are brought back. Afterward, he stops trusting the idea that being careful will keep anyone safe. He begins checking exits in every building, sitting with his back to walls, and scanning every street before stepping outside. Even now, back home, he does it automatically in restaurants and parking lots. He notices where cover might be, where a sound came from, how quickly he could move his wife out of danger. His body reacts before his mind can catch up. A car backfiring on the street sends a bolt of heat through his chest. Helicopter blades overhead make him feel as if he is back in the camp, waiting for the next impact.

When he returns home, his wife is relieved, then puzzled, then hurt by how different he is. He is physically present but distant, spending long stretches on his phone without absorbing anything, or sitting in silence while she talks. He loves her and knows he is not giving her much of himself, which makes him feel ashamed. He becomes irritable with small disruptions and starts avoiding news coverage, foreign aid campaigns, and even conversations about travel. At work, he is still competent, but he struggles with concentration and forgets simple things he used to manage easily. He has trouble editing content because images of suffering trigger a surge of memory that is both emotional and bodily; his stomach knots, his hands go cold, and he has to stand up and walk around before he can think again.

He also notices how much he has changed in private. He cannot watch his niece play with toy soldiers without feeling sick. He wakes sweating from dreams he cannot fully recall, only the feeling of running, hiding, and being unable to help. At times he feels detached from his own life, as if he is watching himself from a distance. He misses the man who left for the assignment, the one who believed purpose alone could protect him. Now he moves through his days with vigilance and fatigue, trying to keep his composure for his wife, his colleagues, and the version of himself that is still trying to hold the whole thing together.
